title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution processed all planned pairs (complete_pair_count = 200) using 200 model calls (one shared deterministic generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. The paired contingency was n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, exact execution accounting, a vetted 10% Mininet holdout that produced zero validator–emulator disagreements, and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity. Canonical archived artifacts (execution bundle) are available to auditors for independent inspection (see Disclosure).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models can increase NetOps productivity but risks producing incorrect or unsafe changes that cause outages or policy violations. Prior work therefore proposes grounding, deterministic validation, and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. The operational benefit of automated repair is conditional on three factors: (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures under the chosen generator/prompting policy; (ii) validator coverage and fidelity; and (iii) the available repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question: Does an automated, deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? The study was designed as a paired experiment that fixes the generator output per task and isolates the marginal effect of invoking a validator+repair on the same candidate.
sections.related_work: LLM deployments in operational domains exhibit factual errors, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism; remedies proposed in the literature include retrieval grounding, deterministic verifiers (e.g., Batfish‑style checkers), and generate–validate–repair architectures. NetOps prototypes show feasibility of intent→configuration synthesis but rarely provide preregistered, externally auditable failure‑rate measurements. Threat and red‑team studies highlight configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injection vectors that can materially change safety outcomes for agentic workflows. Our study contributes an externally auditable, preregistered measurement that isolates the marginal effect of deterministic repair on a fixed generator output, complementing prior prototype, mitigation, and adversarial analyses.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. We preregistered study id cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02 with a paired design (n = 200 tasks), one deterministic shared initial generation per task, and at most one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; the primary test was an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs used 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Sample size planning and power assumptions (baseline ≈30%, targeted 50% relative reduction) are documented in the preregistration; those assumptions did not influence execution decisions after the freeze.

Task bank, validators, and holdout. The confirmatory workload is a curated machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank (200 tasks, four topology clusters). The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces syntactic and intent/constraint checks and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet data‑plane emulator served as a secondary disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator–emulator mismatches; the executed contamination check produced zero disagreement flags on that holdout.

Adapter semantics and runtime determinism reconciliation. The execution bundle declares model: gpt‑5‑mini and includes a model configuration record where temperature is not set. Deterministic shared‑initial generation semantics were enforced at the adapter/orchestration layer (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) rather than by relying on an explicit model temperature field. Evidence of adapter enforcement and single shared invocations is captured in the archived execution reconciliation artifacts: hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0; stage_counts indicate shared_initial_generation = 200; model_calls_used = 200; repair_calls_used = 0; completed_episode_count = 400; complete_pair_count = 200. These recorded counts demonstrate that one deterministic shared generation per task was used for both baseline and guarded conditions, removing sampling variance across conditions by design. We therefore make the causal contrast conditional on the fixed generator output (shared‑initial policy) as preregistered.

Repair policy and handling. If the primary validator reported violations the preregistered policy allowed a single automated repair prompt to the same LLM and a re‑validation step; repaired candidates and repair prompts would be recorded. The adapter‑enforced model‑call cap was 400 (200 initial + up to 200 repairs). Because no initial candidates failed the primary validator in this run, the repair branch was never invoked and repair statistics are absent.

Statistical implementation. The confirmatory test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test applied to the paired contingency (n11, n10, n01, n00). Bootstrap percentile CIs used 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729). Planned sensitivity branches (contamination treatments, missingness handling) were prespecified and would execute if triggered by contamination flags or technical failures.

Reproducibility note. Canonical archived artifacts supporting each major accounting statement are included in the execution bundle (listed in the Disclosure). We also disclose a reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw the Mininet 10% holdout is not present as a labeled artifact, which prevents bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of the exact holdout selection despite the contamination summary reporting zero disagreements.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run executed under the frozen plan (start and end timestamps recorded in the execution manifest). Accounting totals: completed_episode_count = 400, complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task), repair_calls_used = 0, maximum_model_calls = 400. Adapter/provider audit fields record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 200, and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, confirming the preregistered shared_initial enforcement.

Primary outcomes. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% for this workload under the shared‑initial policy, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis is not evaluable on these data.

Mininet holdout and contamination. The preregistered Mininet 10% holdout (20 tasks) produced zero validator–emulator disagreements in the executed contamination check. The contamination detector therefore produced no flags and the conservative exclusion branch was not activated.

Representative diagnostics and difficulty composition. Representative per‑task validator traces confirm that parsed_command_count matched required_command_count and that validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true for inspected examples. The task‑bank difficulty composition observed in the execution bundle is: extreme = 25 tasks (12.5%), very_hard = 100 tasks (50.0%), hard = 50 tasks (25.0%), medium = 25 tasks (12.5%).

Unobserved branches. No repair attempts occurred, so preregistered secondary estimands that depend on repair events are empty in the archived analysis artifacts.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation. The confirmatory outcome is conditional: under the chosen generator/prompting policy and the adapter‑enforced shared_initial design, validator‑detectable failures were absent on the curated workload, so automated repair had no validator‑detected errors to correct. The degenerate paired contingency (no discordant pairs) yields an exact test p = 1.0 and zero bootstrap CI width; this is an exact artifact‑grounded statement, not evidence about repair utility under other sampling or workload regimes.

Methodological tradeoffs. The shared_initial paired design isolates the marginal effect of validating/repairing a fixed generator output but intentionally excludes benefits obtainable by re‑sampling the LLM or by using nonzero temperature diversity. To estimate unconditional operational failure rates and repair utility in an open sampling regime, future confirmatory work should include independent per‑condition sampling and multi‑draw policies, larger repair budgets, and wider emulator coverage.

Validator coverage and operational assurance. Deterministic validators provide necessary but not sufficient safety guarantees: their coverage is task‑dependent and must be corroborated by emulation and adversarial testing. The zero disagreements observed in the 20‑task Mininet holdout is a limited but favorable corroboration for this run; scaling the holdout and publishing holdout selection seeds would strengthen reproducibility and external validity.

Practical implication. Organizations should first measure baseline validator failure prevalence under their intended generation policy. If baseline validator failures are rare, a limited automated repair budget yields limited marginal returns for validator‑detectable errors; resources may be better spent expanding validator fidelity, adversarial testing, or adopting multi‑sample generation to surface latent failures. If baseline failures are nontrivial, a well‑designed GVR with adequate repair budget and richer validators can reduce validator‑detected errors.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini with adapter‑enforced shared_initial semantics and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent on this workload under the enforced sampling policy. The artifact‑grounded outcome highlights that GVR’s marginal value is workload and policy dependent: when validator‑detectable failures are rare, automated repair delivers no measured marginal benefit for those validator‑detected errors. Future work should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, expand validator fidelity and emulation checks, and evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model policies as well as multi‑step repair budgets.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: orchestration used hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the deterministic task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Primary deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator was preregistered and executed as a secondary disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks); the executed contamination check produced zero disagreements on that holdout. Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls. Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan; model calls, prompts, seeds, validator traces, emulator traces, logs, and the artifact manifest are archived in the execution bundle. Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw the Mininet 10% holdout is not present as a labeled artifact in the archive; this absence prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of the drawn holdout despite the contamination summary reporting no disagreements. The canonical execution bundle contains the archived artifacts necessary to audit the claims (see preregistration id).
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested. Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
